newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Onus of cutting HK dealing costs rests on exchange.
newsitem.headline: Onus of cutting HK dealing costs rests on exchange.

text.p: The Hong Kong Stock Exchange's drive to improve competitiveness by cutting transaction costs may rest on the levies collected by market authorities if brokers reject proposals for flexibility on commissions.
"It would be easier for the exchange to reduce the transaction levy than it would be for members to change their commission," a source close to the exchange said on Wednesday.
The transaction levy, imposed by the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), represents more than half of the SFC's income.
"Whether it would be acceptable to the SFC is another matter," the exchange source said.

Earlier in the day, the Hong Kong Stockbrokers Association, which represents 160 of more than 500 members of the exchange, rejected proposals in an exchange consultation paper suggesting the introduction of negotiable commissions on large orders.
Hong Kong transaction costs include a government stamp duty, brokerage commissions, transaction levies and clearing fees.
The minimum broker commission is now 0.25 percent of the value of orders on both the buy and sell side.
The Hong Kong Stock Exchange hopes that lower costs would prompt the government to cut stamp duty on transactions, enhancing the competitiveness of the Hong Kong stock market.

The transaction levy of 0.013 percent is divided between the exchange, which gets 0.007 percent, and the SFC, which gets 0.006 percent. The SFC's 1995/96 revenue amounted to HK$256 million, of which HK$134 million came from the levy.
"The issue of the transaction levy needs to be considered in the broader context of dealing costs and in the budgetary processes of the exchange and the SFC," an SFC spokesman said.
He said the commission was in favour of lower dealing costs.
"We are still in discussion with both the government and the exchange about how best to accomplish that," he said.

"I would not rule out the possibility of brokerage commissions being reduced. People do say that worldwde they are quite low already but in some cases, in practice, firms are offering lower than the rate for larger transactions."
The stock exchange had been hoping to resolve the matter before the government finalises plans for this year's budget due in March.
"Every year we say that a reduction would definitely help the Hong Kong market," an exchange spokesman said.
A government spokesman said any proposals put forward by the exchange to reduce the stamp duty would be considered.
"If the commission and fees charged on transactions become lower, then obviously there is a case for the government to lower the stamp duty," he said.

"The various parties including the government have now begun to study the fee structure. Whether we reduce the stamp duty or the commission and also the transaction fees -- these need to be looked at in total rather than separately."
But the government spokesman declined to say whether a reduction in the stamp duty was an issue in this year's budget.
"The Financial Secretary will talk about a lot of things that will affect the financial sector, to the benefit of the financial sector I presume," he said.

Hong Kong Stockbrokers Association chairman Cheung Tin-sang said the association had voted on Tuesday to keep the current commission structure unchanged. The association represents mostly small- and medium-sized brokerages.
Lower commissions may improve market turnover but would mean a loss of income for medium-sized firms, he said.
"The proposal of cutting commissions is purely not pragmatic," he said.
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6345
